g.text: Toy Models of Superposition & Sparse Autoencoders
Anthropic's toy-model paper reproduced end-to-end: how neural networks pack more features than dimensions, then how SAEs unpack the superposition.
Follows the notebook flow exactly: Part 1 Nonprivileged Basis -> Part 2 Privileged Basis -> Part 3 Feature Geometry -> Part 4 Deep Double Descent -> Part 5 SAEs.
Math intuition marked ∂ (blue). Prereq / concept boxes marked ★ (yellow). Q&A boxes marked Q (dark orange). Code cards use mono font. All notes in first person.
Big picture + reading plan (following the notebook)
Superposition = representing MORE features than dimensions by encoding each feature in a NON-orthogonal direction. Interference is tolerable when features are sparse.
28 sections + takeaways. Structure follows the notebook's 5-part progression exactly.
§1 Q&A: four foundational questions from the notebook (privileged basis, superposition vs polysemanticity, importance+sparsity, feature)
§2 Glossary of key concepts WITH mini-diagrams (feature, polysemanticity, monosemanticity, superposition, privileged basis, bottleneck, interference, shrinkage)
§3 ToyModel architecture: h = W x, x' = ReLU(W^T h + b)
§4 Non-privileged basis: why W and (O W) give the same model
§6 Training data examples: concrete batches (independent features)
§10 Training dynamics: what the 4 animation HTMLs show
§11 METRICS for observing polysemanticity (Frobenius, ||W_i||, D_i, cosine similarity)
§12 2D geometry results: pentagons + W^T W heatmaps
§13 NeuronModel: privileged basis via h = ReLU(W x)
§17 Dimensionality D_i + polytope zoo + sticky points
§18 Memorising vs generalising as competing superpositions
§27 Standard vs Gated vs JumpReLU comparison table
Notebook cell-output PNGs are embedded INLINE inside the relevant sections above:
§7 (correlated / anticorrelated / 3-pair) §12 (2D geometry results) §18 (Deep Double Descent) §21 (SAE training).
Before running any code, we should be able to answer these four questions from the notebook.
Q: What is a privileged basis? Why are neurons privileged but the residual stream is not?
A privileged basis is one where the STANDARD BASIS DIRECTIONS are meaningful (due to the structure
of computation). Does NOT mean the basis is interpretable - just that basis directions are special.
Something is a privileged basis iff it is NOT rotation-independent.
NEURONS are privileged because ReLU (or any elementwise nonlinearity) acts INDEPENDENTLY on each
standard basis coord. Rotating the basis turns ReLU into an entangled function of the new coords
(interference between components). So model behavior changes under rotation. Rows of W_in are
RESIDUAL STREAM is NOT privileged because everything reading from it and writing to it is a LINEAR
map. We could apply W_out -> W_out R and W_in -> R^-1 W_in for any invertible R and the model's
computation is unchanged. The residual-stream basis is arbitrary.
You can't claim 'resid_stream[47] encodes plurality' - any basis direction could equally well be
the encoding, rotated & distributed across many.
COMMON MISCONCEPTION: 'privileged = interpretable'. FALSE. Privileged basis is NECESSARY for
interpretability (you need meaningful directions), but NOT SUFFICIENT (meaningful != readable).
Q: What is the difference between superposition and polysemanticity?
POLYSEMANTICITY = one neuron encoding multiple features. Not a problem by itself - there could exist
SOME basis for features where each basis vector maps to a single feature.
SUPERPOSITION = representing MORE features than there are dimensions. This IMPLIES polysemanticity
(by pigeonhole: features > dims -> some dim carries >1 feature), but the converse is NOT true.
POLYSEMANTICITY (features > 1 per neuron) does NOT imply SUPERPOSITION.
Why the distinction matters: an SAE with d_sae >= n_features can UNDO polysemanticity even if the
model has superposition, by rotating into a wider (overcomplete) sparse code.
Q: What are importance and sparsity of features? Do you expect more polysemantic neurons at higher sparsity?
IMPORTANCE I_i = how much feature i matters for lowering the loss. Coefficient in weighted MSE:
L = sum over i of I_i * (x_i - x_i')^2
SPARSITY S = how frequently feature i is ZERO in the input. Feature probability p = 1 - S.
For S close to 1, features fire rarely.
As SPARSITY INCREASES, we get MORE polysemantic neurons. Why:
When features rarely co-occur, cross-talk between shared dims rarely matters. A single neuron can
safely encode several sparse features. Interference only hurts when both features are active
simultaneously, and if features are sparse enough, that's negligible.
So: HIGH SPARSITY => more features packed per neuron => more polysemantic => more superposition.
This is the fundamental reason real LLMs (which handle very sparse features) exhibit dramatic
superposition, while small toy models with dense inputs barely show any.
Q: How would you define a feature?
No single agreed definition. Most are unfortunately CIRCULAR ('a feature is a thing represented by
a neuron'). Two common non-circular definitions:
'A feature is a PROPERTY of an input to the model, or some SUBSET of that input (e.g. a token in a
prompt, a patch of an image).'
'A feature is a SCALAR FUNCTION of the input. In this essay, neural network features are directions,
often simply individual neurons. A MEANINGFUL FEATURE is one that genuinely responds to an
articulable property of the input, such as the presence of a curve or a floppy ear.'
For our purposes: a feature = a coordinate of the input vector x. It's an abstract 'attribute' the
model MIGHT want to represent. Whether it does depends on importance + sparsity + capacity.
Reference these throughout the rest of the diagram. Each concept has a visual explanation next to its definition.
Consistent with Neel Nanda's mech-interp glossary (https://www.neelnanda.io/mechanistic-interpretability/glossary).

TMS: Superposition in a Nonprivileged Basis
ToyModel architecture: x -> W -> h -> W^T -> +b -> ReLU -> x'
The canonical Anthropic toy model. 5-dim input x, maps down to 2-dim h via W, maps back up via W^T, adds a bias, ReLU.
TIED WEIGHTS: W and W^T are the SAME parameter, so we're really fitting x' approx x through a rank-2 bottleneck.
Architecture: tensor shapes at every stage
Compact: x' = ReLU( W^T (W x) + b_final ) = ReLU( (W^T W) x + b_final )
W has shape (d_hidden, n_features) = (2, 5). W^T W has shape (5, 5) = the INTERFERENCE MATRIX.
Diagonal (W^T W)[i, i] = ||W_:,i||^2 = how much feature i is represented.
Off-diagonal (W^T W)[i, j] = W_:,i . W_:,j = interference between features i and j.
n_inst: int # parallel independent models (batch dim for weights)
n_features: int = 5 # F: number of possible features
'... inst feats, inst hidden feats -> ... inst hidden')
'... inst hidden, inst hidden feats -> ... inst feats')
Non-privileged basis: W and (O W) are the SAME model
Without ReLU on hidden, the effective op is linear. ANY orthogonal rotation of W gives an identical model.
This is why individual rows of W ('hidden neurons') have no meaning - the basis is arbitrary.
Take orthogonal matrix O (O^T O = I).
h' = O W x = O h
x'' = ReLU((O W)^T (O W) x + b_final)
= ReLU(W^T O^T O W x + b_final)
So training could converge to W OR to O W (for any orthogonal O).
The INTERFERENCE STRUCTURE W^T W is the only thing that matters.
Individual columns of W have arbitrary orientation.
★ Consequence: real-world analog is the residual stream
The residual stream in a transformer is EXACTLY this
situation. Everything reading from the residual
uses a linear map (Q, K, V, W_in, W_out). We can
rotate the residual basis by any O:
For every reader: W_read -> W_read O^-1
For every writer: W_write -> O W_write
O composes away in every read-then-write. Model's
function is unchanged. So basis directions in the
residual stream have NO INHERENT MEANING.
You can't ask 'what does resid[47] encode?'.
Those ARE meaningful because they're baked into
SAE latents ARE meaningful for the same reason:
their decoder direction W_dec[i] is a fixed
rotation-specific vector, not a basis coordinate.
Two rotations of W, same model behavior (same W^T W)
Sampling + importance: the two dials that drive geometry
SPARSITY S = P(feature is zero). Feature probability p = 1 - S. IMPORTANCE I_i weights per-feature MSE in the loss.
Together they determine what the trained W looks like: which features get represented, and what geometry they take.
'''(batch, n_inst, n_features) - uniform features in [0, 1] times a Bernoulli present-mask.'''
# Random magnitudes IF feature fires. Uniform [0, 1].
# Bernoulli mask: feature fires with prob self.feature_probability.
feat_is_present = feat_seeds <= self.feature_probability # broadcast: (n_inst, F) -> (B, n_inst, F)
Two competing forces in the model:
Every feature we ignore costs I_i.
both fire. Cost is proportional to
So the tradeoff SKEWS toward representing more
Training data examples: what generate_batch produces
Concrete batches showing what the model sees during training. Rows = examples, columns = features, values = magnitudes in [0, 1] (or [-1, 1] for §14).
Zero = feature not present. The sampling pattern DIRECTLY drives what the model learns.
Features 0 and 1 fire TOGETHER (or both absent).
EXACTLY ONE of features 0, 1 fires per row.
∂ Co-occurrence probability drives the model's choice of geometry
The KEY metric that drives model behavior is P(both features fire simultaneously) = co-occurrence probability:
INDEPENDENT (p=0.2): P(i and j both fire) = p * p = 0.04 Interference matters 4% of the time.
CORRELATED (0, 1): P(0 and 1 both fire) = p = 0.20 Interference matters 20% of the time.
ANTICORRELATED (0, 1): P(0 and 1 both fire) = 0 = 0.00 Interference NEVER matters.
Independent -> spread out (pentagon, etc.) - minimize total interference across all pairs.
Correlated -> ORTHOGONAL - pair fires together 20% of the time, so interference is expensive.
Anticorrelated -> ANTIPODAL - never both fire, so opposite directions with sign disambiguation is free.
The model's LEARNED geometry depends on how features CO-OCCUR, not just how often they marginally fire.
Correlated pair -> ORTHOGONAL directions. Anticorrelated -> ANTIPODAL.
Correlated pair: fire TOGETHER (or both absent)
seed ~ Bernoulli(p) # ONE shared seed per pair
x_j = mag_j * seed # both use same on/off
Consequence: always both active or both inactive.
Interference between them matters WHENEVER they
fire (which is ALL the time they fire).
the model gives them independent dims if possible.
which_i ~ Bernoulli(0.5) # if yes, which one
When i fires: h moves in +direction.
When j fires: h moves in -direction.
Sign of h disambiguates which fired.
Real-world: 'is Python' vs 'is teen vampire fic'.
Notebook cell 57 output: Correlated feature pairs (blue pair + green pair)
Feature 0, 1 (blue) fire TOGETHER. Feature 2, 3 (green) fire together. Each pair has its own probability.
Observed geometry: each PAIR takes an ORTHOGONAL direction in 2D. Within a pair, features are at ~90°
so they don't interfere when both fire. Across pairs, geometry varies with sparsity.
Notebook cell 60 output: Anticorrelated pairs (features 0, 1 mutually exclusive; features 2, 3 too)
Anticorrelated means: EXACTLY ONE of the pair fires per example, or neither. Never both.
Observed geometry: ANTIPODAL pairs. Feature 0 and feature 1 point in opposite directions (W_0 = -W_1).
Sign of h[i] disambiguates which one of the pair fired. Two features share ONE dim (D = 1/2).
Notebook cell 61 output: 3 correlated pairs (6 features packed into 2D)
3 pairs, each with its own probability. 6 total features to pack into 2D.
Instead of a hexagon, we see 3 pairs at ~120° apart, with each pair internally orthogonal.
Total: 3 pair-directions in 2D -> interference within a pair (correlated -> ok) but not between pairs.
Standard MSE weighted by per-feature importance I_i. Mean over batch and features, sum over instances.
The weighting is the key: it tells the model 'don't spend capacity on unimportant features'.
L(x, x') = (1 / (B * F)) * sum over batch b * sum over feature i [ I_i * (x_b_i - x'_b_i)^2 ]
B = batch size, F = n_features, I_i = importance of feature i (a fixed per-feature weight).
- MEAN over BATCH and FEATURES (standard MSE convention - LR insensitive to B, F)
- SUM over INSTANCES (each instance trains at same rate as if solo)
Why mean-over-features, not sum? Otherwise doubling n_features would double the loss magnitude
even with the same per-feature error. Mean normalizes this.
Why sum-over-instances? Each instance is an independent model. Summing their losses gives Adam
the same gradient magnitude on each instance's weights as if it were training alone.
loss = einops.reduce(err, 'batch inst feats -> inst', 'mean') # mean over batch + feats
Standard Adam optimizer. The exercises use LEARNING RATE SCHEDULES that decay over training.
Notice: n_inst instances trained SIMULTANEOUSLY in a single loop. All instances see the same optimizer.
def cosine_decay_lr(step, steps): return np.cos(0.5 * np.pi * step / (steps - 1))
The optimizer LR is scaled by these functions each step. Standard choice: linear_lr or cosine_decay_lr.
▶ How this training loop differs from typical ML
Notice: we re-sample the training batch EVERY STEP. There is no fixed dataset. This means the
model sees potentially unlimited data - it can't overfit in the usual sense. Instead it learns the
underlying feature distribution p(x) directly from samples.
The n_inst instances share NO gradients - each has its own W, b_final, and gets its own gradient update.
This is like running n_inst separate trainings in parallel, but efficiently on GPU via batched matmuls.
Training dynamics: what the 4 animation HTMLs show
Four d3.js scatter animations in this directory visualise W or W_dec evolving over 200 training steps.
Each demonstrates a different training regime. Watch to build intuition for how superposition emerges.

Each metric tells us a different aspect: how many features, how orthogonal, how well recovered.

For each true feature j and SAE latent i:
Perfect: cos = 1.0 for one latent per
features have at least one aligned

This is THE metric for detecting

How ORTHOGONAL are the features? -> W^T W off-diagonal values
What geometry did the model pick? -> Per-feature dimensionality D_i (§17 sticky points)

2D geometry results: pentagons + W^T W heatmaps
Sweeping sparsity, the columns of W arrange themselves into REGULAR polygons.
The 5x5 W^T W matrix visualises the interference structure. Diagonal = per-feature strength, off-diag = pairwise cos * norm * norm.
∂ W^T W math: interference matrix in one page
(W^T W)[i, j] = sum_h W[h, i] * W[h, j] = <feature-i-vector, feature-j-vector>
(W^T W)[i, i] = ||W[:, i]||^2 = squared norm of feature-i's 2D vector.
1 if feature is represented (unit column), 0 if dropped.
0 if orthogonal, +1 if parallel, -1 if antipodal.
Reading W^T W tells you: which features are represented (diag), which pairs interfere (off-diag),
and the whole geometry. It's THE summary of a trained bottleneck model.
Notebook cell 16 output: Cosine similarities of 5 random 2D feature embeddings
The 5x5 heatmap of W^T W for a RANDOM (untrained) W of shape (2, 5), columns L2-normalized.
Diagonal is exactly 1 (unit norm). Off-diagonals are NON-ZERO -> interference.
This is what INTERFERENCE looks like at initialization: features are non-orthogonal, dot products aren't zero.
Notebook cell 37 output: THE key plot - 5 feature vectors in 2D across 8 sparsity levels (1-S = feature probability)
Left = DENSE (1-S=1.0, all features fire). Right = SPARSE (1-S=0.02, features rarely fire).
At dense: only the 2 MOST IMPORTANT features get non-zero norm. Others collapse to origin (dropped).
At sparse: all 5 features get unit norm, arranged as a PENTAGON at 72° apart.
Colors: darker = more important feature. Important features keep unit norm across all sparsity levels.
Notebook cell 40 output: 200 batch datapoints projected into 2D hidden space, at each sparsity level
Same 8 instances as above, but plotting h = W x for 200 random x's (not the feature vectors themselves).
At HIGH sparsity: batch points cluster ALONG the feature directions (pentagon spokes) because each
example has only 1 active feature. At LOW sparsity: points fill 2D space more uniformly.
Visually confirms that sparse features can be RECOVERED by projecting h onto the feature directions.
TMS: Superposition in a Privileged Basis
Privileged basis: h = ReLU(W x) -> hidden basis MEANS something
Add a ReLU on the hidden layer. The basis is now privileged - individual neurons carry identity.
This mimics real transformer MLP hidden layers: nonlinearity between W_in and W_out is what makes neurons privileged.
NeuronModel architecture: ReLU sandwiched between W and W^T
Compact: h = ReLU(W x) x' = ReLU(W^T h + b_final)
The hidden ReLU makes the model NOT rotation-equivariant -> individual neurons (rows of W) have identity.
∂ The math: ReLU breaks rotation invariance
The mathematical reason ReLU makes the basis privileged:
In the STANDARD basis, ReLU acts elementwise:
ReLU([x, y]) = [max(x, 0), max(y, 0)] Each coord treated INDEPENDENTLY.
In a ROTATED basis x' = (x+y)/sqrt(2), y' = (x-y)/sqrt(2), ReLU becomes ENTANGLED:
So the rotated 'ReLU' is a COMPLETELY DIFFERENT function of x', y'. It's no longer elementwise.
The standard basis is SPECIAL (privileged). Rows of W_in point in specific directions that ReLU
treats independently. Individual neuron activations carry meaningful identity.
Contrast: without ReLU, everything downstream reads via linear maps, and any rotation gets 'absorbed'
by adjusting other weights. No privileged basis. Individual coordinates are meaningless.
'''Same architecture but with a ReLU on the hidden layer. Privileged basis.'''
# NEW: ReLU on the hidden state - creates a privileged basis for neurons.
'... inst feats, inst d_hidden feats -> ... inst d_hidden'))
'... inst d_hidden, inst d_hidden feats -> ... inst feats')
# NOTE: reconstruction is trivial. Identity is LINEAR - model can shift biases so hidden
# activations are always positive -> ReLU never fires -> effectively linear. §14 fixes this by
# using |x| as the target, which CANNOT be represented without the ReLU firing.
Computation in superposition: compute |x| for signed x
NeuronModel task was reconstruct-x, which is LINEAR - model bypasses ReLU via bias shift. To study COMPUTATION we need a nonlinear task.
Use |x| for x in [-1, 1]. Since |x| = ReLU(x) + ReLU(-x), the ReLU MUST fire. Now we can study computation-in-superposition.
NeuronComputationModel architecture: W1 and W2 are INDEPENDENT (untied)
Forward: h = ReLU(W1 x) x' = ReLU(W2 h + b_final) Target: |x|
Loss: L = sum_i I_i (|x_i| - x'_i)^2 (weighted MSE against absolute value)
∂ Why |x| is the right test task
Why |x| forces the ReLU to matter:
1. Identity function x -> x is LINEAR. A model with a ReLU hidden layer can BYPASS ReLU by
shifting biases so all hidden values are positive. Then ReLU acts as identity.
2. Absolute value x -> |x| is genuinely nonlinear (kinked at 0). CANNOT be represented by
any linear model. The ReLU is FORCED to fire on the negative side.
3. Fortunately, abs is easy to build from ReLU:
Monosemantic solution: 2 neurons per feature (one for +half, one for -half).
5 features * 2 neurons = 10 neurons monosemantic. We only have d_hidden=5 (or fewer)
4. At LOW sparsity, each feature gets its dedicated 2 neurons.
At MEDIUM sparsity, neurons start being SHARED across features (asymmetric motif in §15).
At HIGH sparsity, many features per neuron, complex clean-up circuitry.
'''W1 and W2 are INDEPENDENT (unlike ToyModel's tied W). Computes |x| for x in [-1, 1].'''
W2: Float[Tensor, 'inst n_features d_hidden'] # decoder: 5x2 (SEPARATE from W1)
'... inst feats, inst d_hidden feats -> ... inst d_hidden'))
'... inst d_hidden, inst n_features d_hidden -> ... inst n_features') + self.b_final)
err = self.importance * (out - batch.abs()).pow(2) # TARGET IS ABS(x)
A single neuron encoding two features with UNEQUAL W1 magnitudes and FLIPPED W2 magnitudes. Creates cross-feature leakage.
The model corrects it with an auxiliary neuron using the terminal ReLU truncation.
The asymmetric motif in a single shared neuron (L = 'large', S = 'small')
SETUP: neuron k detects feature i with W1[k,i]=L (large) and feature j with W1[k,j]=S (small)
Output weights are FLIPPED: W2[i,k]=S, W2[j,k]=L
x'_i = L*S*x_i = correct x'_j = L*L*x_i = WAY TOO LARGE
Corrective neuron detects i, subtracts from
x'_j -> negative -> terminal ReLU clamps to 0
∂ Full math of the asymmetric motif + why it's asymmetric
Consider shared neuron k. Let L = 'large', S = 'small' (values >> 1 and << 1 respectively).
W1[k, i] = L, W1[k, j] = S (input weights: neuron k listens more to i)
W2[i, k] = S, W2[j, k] = L (output weights: FLIPPED)
Neuron activation: a_k = ReLU( L*x_i + S*x_j )
Downstream output: x'_i = S * a_k x'_j = L * a_k
CASE A (only i active, x_i > 0, x_j = 0):
a_k = L * x_i -> x'_i = L*S*x_i = CORRECT x'_j = L*L*x_i = TOO LARGE <- PROBLEM
CASE B (only j active, x_j > 0, x_i = 0):
a_k = S * x_j -> x'_i = S*S*x_j ~= 0 x'_j = S*L*x_j = CORRECT
THE FIX: another neuron k' with W1[k', i] = M and W2[j, k'] = -N (NEGATIVE) so it subtracts from
x'_j when only i is active. MN = L^2 -> cancels the spurious signal.
WHY ASYMMETRIC: the corrective neuron pushes x'_j NEGATIVE when only i fires. Terminal ReLU on x'
TRUNCATES the correction to 0 if it overshoots. Works one way only! Reversing (i, j) roles would
produce a big POSITIVE overshoot that ReLU wouldn't truncate. Hence 'asymmetric'.
Frobenius norm ||W||_F^2 = number of features represented
The FIRST metric for measuring what the model learned. Total 'capacity' spent on features.
Full derivation from scratch, showing how column norms map to feature counts.
DEFINITION. Squared Frobenius norm of matrix W:
||W||_F^2 = sum over all entries W[i, j]^2
DERIVATION. Why does this equal 'number of features represented'?
Rewrite the sum as a sum over COLUMNS of W:
||W||_F^2 = sum over j (feature index) [ sum over i (hidden dim) of W[i, j]^2 ]
= sum over j of ||W[:, j]||^2 (squared column norm)
where W_j = W[:, j] is the 2D vector representing feature j.
OBSERVATION. If the model represents feature j, we expect the trained ||W_j|| ~ 1 (unit vector).
If the model DROPS feature j (assigns it no capacity), ||W_j|| ~ 0.
So ||W||_F^2 ~ (number of represented features). It's a soft integer count.
Not exactly an integer - some features may be partially represented (D between 0 and 1) - but the
trend is clear: as sparsity grows, ||W||_F^2 climbs past d_hidden up toward n_features.
||W||_F^2 / m vs sparsity (fraction of features represented)
At dense (sparsity=0): only d_hidden/m features represented = 0.4 for our 2/5 model.
Smooth sigmoidal rise as sparsity increases -> capacity gained via superposition.
Dimensionality D_i: per-feature geometry with sticky points
The SECOND metric. D_i = 'fraction of a hidden dim allocated to feature i'. Sticky at specific rationals.
Each sticky point corresponds to a specific REGULAR POLYTOPE arrangement of feature vectors.
D_i = ||W_i||^2 / sum over j of ( W_i_hat . W_j )^2
where W_i = column of W for feature i, W_i_hat = W_i / ||W_i|| = unit vector along W_i.
D_i >= 0 with equality iff ||W_i|| = 0 (feature not represented).
D_i <= 1 with equality iff W_i is ORTHOGONAL to all W_j (j != i).
[because j=i term equals ||W_i||^2, the largest possible term]
sum over i of D_i <= d_hidden (total 'used capacity' can't exceed d_hidden).
INTERPRETATION. 'fraction of a hidden dimension' allocated to feature i. D_i near 1 means feature
has essentially its own direction. D_i = 1/k means it shares a subspace with k-1 others.
The polytope zoo: feature geometries and their D values
The empirical D-vs-sparsity plot from Anthropic's paper (schematic)
Trajectory: as sparsity increases -> features 'jump' between sticky points

Deep Double Descent: memorising vs generalising
Train on a FIXED batch (repeat every step). Sweep batch size. Test loss has a SPIKE between two regimes.
Small batch = memorise DATAPOINTS in superposition. Large batch = generalise FEATURES in superposition. The spike is the transition.
The model packs each DATAPOINT into a superposed
direction of h. Columns of W align with specific
Test loss: HIGH (new datapoints don't match)
This is superposition of DATAPOINTS. Each
datapoint is 'a thing to represent', mutually
Weight decay is critical - without it, memorising
grows weight norms unbounded and always wins.
The model packs each FEATURE into a superposed
direction. Columns of W align with underlying
Test loss: LOW (new datapoints REUSE features)
This is standard superposition of FEATURES -
Weight decay stops memorising from winning by
penalising large weight norms. Features can be
The double-descent curve: test loss vs batch size
▶ How to reproduce the SPIKE + why weight decay matters
SETUP (critical): FIX a batch of size B, then TRAIN MANY STEPS on that SAME batch. Sweep B.
- Very small B: memorising is easier (few things to memorize). Train low, test high.
- Very large B: generalising is easier (features are shared across examples). Both low.
- Between: neither strategy dominates cleanly, and the transition SPIKES the test loss.
NOT the classical overparameterization double-descent - this is a data-size double-descent. But
the mechanism (two competing representations) is analogous, and Anthropic argues it's fundamental.
Uses AdamW with WEIGHT_DECAY = 1e-2. Weight decay constrains ||W|| so memorization can't just
'grow weights' to fit any batch - forcing the model to actually pick between representations.
Notebook cell 110 output: Random illustration (no training) - baseline for what the plot looks like
Random tensor scatter. Feature vectors (top row, blue) and data points (bottom row, red).

Notebook cell 116 output: Double Descent & Superposition (1000 features) - THE key result

★ Notation: neurons vs features vs SAE latents (from notebook cell 123)
The SAE's hidden activations go by MANY NAMES in the literature. Try not to get confused:
NEURONS - they have an activation function applied, making them a privileged basis (like MLP
neurons). Common in older papers. Also used for 'neuron resampling'.
FEATURES - the SAE tries to disentangle features FROM the packed h. Confusing because we
also use 'feature' for the ORIGINAL model's x.
SAE LATENTS - what we use. Neutral, correct. Doesn't overload 'feature' or 'neuron'.
The word 'feature' is [overloaded] (see notebook link) - it can mean:
(a) an attribute of the input data itself,
(b) a direction in the model's activation space,
We'll say SAE LATENT for (c) throughout to keep things clear.
SAE architecture diagram: h -> z -> h'
8-stage tensor flow. Encoder centers h by b_dec, projects via W_enc + b_enc, ReLUs into sparse latent code z.
Decoder projects back via W_dec, adds b_dec back. b_dec acts as a LEARNED CENTER of the h-distribution.
SAE architecture: every stage with shape annotations
∂ SAE forward + loss + why we normalize W_dec
h_cent = h - b_dec # center h by learned mean
pi = einsum(h_cent, W_enc) + b_enc # (batch, inst, d_sae) preactivation
+ lambda * sum_i (||W_dec[i, :]|| * |z_i|) # L1 on z, SCALED BY DECODER ROW NORM
Why scale L1 by decoder row norm:
Without it, the model can 'cheat' by scaling z DOWN and W_dec UP (same h_hat, smaller |z|, smaller
sparsity loss). Scaling L1 by ||W_dec[i, :]|| removes this degree of freedom.
Alternative: normalize W_dec rows to unit norm during forward, then use plain ||z||_1.
In code: W_dec_normalized is a property that does this normalization.
★ Prereq: why normalize W_dec (from notebook cell 130)
From the notebook (cell 130): 'Why do we need W_dec_normalized?'
We normalize W_dec to stop the model from CHEATING.
Imagine if we didn't normalize. The model could make W_enc 10x smaller and W_dec 10x larger.
- Outputs stay the same (reconstruction error is constant).
- The L1 sparsity loss shrinks - the model 'gets away with' having no sparsity.
L2-normalizing W_dec's columns also makes latent magnitudes cleanly interpretable:
they answer 'how much of each unit-length feature is present in h?'
b_dec acts as a LEARNED CENTER of the h-distribution.
Sequence: h_cent = h - b_dec -> encode -> z -> decode -> add b_dec back.
- W_enc doesn't waste capacity encoding the MEAN of h - only the DEVIATIONS.
- Sparsity penalty acts on the DEVIATIONS. 'Being like the mean' costs nothing.
- For a 'typical' h, most latents = 0 and h_hat ~= b_dec is a good baseline.

▲ What actually happens during SAE training (from cell 143)
From notebook cell 143 - IMPORTANT observations about SAE training:
The autoencoder is generally successful at reconstructing h. Sometimes it learns the FULL
MONOSEMANTIC solution (one latent per feature). But MORE OFTEN it learns a COMBINATION of:
1. POLYSEMANTIC LATENTS - fire more frequently than target feature_probability (~2.5%).
They fire on MORE THAN ONE feature.
2. DEAD LATENTS - never activate (fraction of datapoints active = 0).
These are a BIG PROBLEM: no gradients -> don't self-correct.
3. MONOSEMANTIC LATENTS - fire at or slightly BELOW the target probability.
These are the good ones. Each latches onto ONE feature.
You can DIAGNOSE which is which by plotting frac_active per latent over training. See §22 (resampling).
Rare best case: all 5 latents in some instance fall into category 3, uniformly spaced around 2D hidden dim.
Notebook cell 140 output: SAE decoder vectors AFTER training (16 instances)
Each subplot = one SAE instance after training. Dots = SAE decoder columns W_dec[i].
GOOD instances: 5 dots arranged as a pentagon - all 5 features recovered MONOSEMANTICALLY.
BAD instances: some dots clustered together (polysemantic) or at origin (DEAD latents).
This is EXACTLY why resampling matters (§22): dead latents like the ones you see here get reinitialized to hard examples.
Resampling dead latents: simple vs advanced
Dead latents don't self-correct - no gradients flow through them. Solution: periodically REINITIALIZE them to hard examples.
Two algorithms: SIMPLE (random vectors) and ADVANCED (loss-weighted sampling). Advanced is the Anthropic paper's algorithm.
# Dead if never fired in whole window
- Random direction might land on already-covered
# Match ENCODER scale to average of ALIVE latents
PROS: resampled latents land ON hard examples,
Replacement direction random vector hard-example h (loss-weighted)
Encoder scale fixed hyperparameter resample_scale adaptive: matches alive-latent norm
Sampling distribution uniform (n_dead random vecs) Categorical(prob = L2_loss^2 / sum)
Efficiency may hit already-covered features targets under-served features
Uses a sliding window of frac_active over the last N steps.
Dead latents = frac_active < 1e-8 across the ENTIRE window.
Standard: 4 resamplings over 25000 training steps (at t = 2500, 5000, 7500, 10000).
After 10000 steps, dead latents are usually FIXED - no more resampling needed.
- Reconstruction loss BRIEFLY SPIKES right after resampling (new weights don't fit yet).
- Recovers within ~200-500 steps to lower than pre-resampling levels.
- Overall final loss is better than without resampling.
Shrinkage: the L1 penalty biases activations toward zero
STANDARD SAE loss: ||h - h_hat||^2 + lambda * ||z||_1. L1 is useful (drives sparsity) but ALSO shrinks all activations, including the ones that should be big.
This is a SYSTEMATIC bias, not noise. Gated and JumpReLU SAEs are designed to eliminate it.
∂ The math of shrinkage - full derivation
TOY EXAMPLE. Suppose the true feature magnitude for feature i on some input is 1.0. The ideal SAE has:
But the loss has two terms:
where z_i_optimal is the value we'd want (h . W_dec[i, :] / ||W_dec[i, :]||^2).
SHRINKAGE: the optimal z_i is BIASED DOWN by lambda / (2 * ||W_dec[i, :]||^2).
L1 pulls even the 'correct' z_i toward zero.
This is not just noise - it's a SYSTEMATIC UNDERSHOOT. Reconstruction is consistently too small.
The model tries to compensate by growing W_dec norms, but that gets penalized (via row-norm-
scaled L1), so the tradeoff never resolves cleanly.
Visual: bimodal distribution of pre-activations + why threshold activations help
▶ How Gated and JumpReLU SAEs fix shrinkage
1. GATED SAE (see §24): decouple the BINARY GATE (which fires) from the CONTINUOUS MAGNITUDE.
Put L1 penalty on the GATE only. Magnitude has NO L1 -> no shrinkage.
2. JUMPRELU SAE (see §25): use a THRESHOLD activation z * H(z - theta) with learned theta.
Below theta -> exactly 0. Above theta -> exactly z (no shrinkage). Penalize L0, not L1.
Both approaches say: 'L1 penalty was doing two jobs (choosing sparsity + choosing magnitude), and it
does neither well. Separate the jobs.'
Gated SAE: decouple binary gate from continuous magnitude
Two paths: a GATE path decides IF a latent fires (binary, via Heaviside). A MAGNITUDE path decides HOW STRONG (continuous, ReLU).
L1 penalty goes on the GATE preactivation only. Magnitude has NO L1 -> no shrinkage. Auxiliary loss prevents degenerate gate-off solutions.
Gated SAE architecture: two paths from h_cent to f(x)
Gated SAE formulas (DeepMind paper, Appendix G notation):
pi_gate(x) = W_gate h_cent + b_gate # gate preactivation
pi_mag(x) = W_mag h_cent + b_mag # magnitude preactivation
Magnitude and gate share direction; each latent has learned per-latent scale r_mag[i].
Almost equivalent to JumpReLU with parameterized threshold (see §25).
where h_hat_aux = W_dec.detach() * ReLU(pi_gate) + b_dec.detach() (DETACHED decoder)
The auxiliary loss forces the GATE path to be capable of reconstructing on its own, preventing
degenerate solutions where gate is always 0 and magnitude compensates (or vice versa).
JumpReLU SAE: threshold activation + L0 penalty via STE
Same architecture as standard SAE, but the activation is JumpReLU_theta(z) = z * H(z - theta). Learned per-latent threshold theta.
Penalize L0 directly (not L1). Backprop through Heaviside via straight-through estimator with rectangle kernel.
L0 counts nonzero z entries. Directly encourages
sparsity WITHOUT shrinking the surviving z values.
★ Bonus: targeting a specific L0 value (from notebook cell 174)
You can target a specific L0 sparsity value by using the squared difference between L0 and the target:
The exercises don't implement this, but it's a natural extension once you have JumpReLU working.
This lets you say 'I want exactly ~5 active latents per input' rather than 'as sparse as possible'.
STE intuitions: WHY the rectangle kernel gives correct gradients
Two ways to see why using a bump function K as the fake derivative of Heaviside is right.
(1) FUNCTIONAL: it's the derivative of a sharp CDF approximating the step. (2) PROBABILISTIC: it's a KDE of the expected-loss derivative.
PROBLEM: Both ||z||_0 = sum_i H(z_pre_i - theta_i) AND JumpReLU itself contain discontinuous Heaviside.
Gradients wrt theta_i are 0 almost everywhere (undefined at the jump).
The model CANNOT learn theta via normal backprop.
SOLUTION: STRAIGHT-THROUGH ESTIMATORS (STEs). Replace the true (=0 or undefined) gradient with a
bump-function approximation that has the CORRECT INTEGRAL over the jump.
d/d theta H(z - theta) := -(1 / eps) * K( (z - theta) / eps )
d/d theta JumpReLU_theta(z) := -(theta / eps) * K( (z - theta) / eps )
K is a KERNEL: a probability density (non-negative, integrates to 1, centered at 0, finite variance).
eps is the kernel bandwidth (~0.001). Small = sharp, faithful to jump location.
Functional: CDF approximates step, K is its pdf
Integral of K over region = 1 (jump size).
STE = KDE of p(z) around theta.
Batch-avg STE = unbiased estimator of true gradient.
return z * (z > theta).float() # exact JumpReLU: z * H(z - theta)
'''For L0 penalty with STE gradient wrt theta.'''
Standard vs Gated vs JumpReLU: side-by-side comparison
Three SAE architectures. Same input h, same reconstruction goal. Different activation + loss.
The best choice depends on your task: simplicity (JumpReLU), stability (Gated), or bare baseline (Standard).
▶ Choosing an SAE variant for your project
Standard SAE: Fastest to implement. Baseline for comparison. Shrinkage limits reconstruction quality.
Good when you just want SOMETHING working and don't care about fine reconstruction detail.
Gated SAE: Best reconstruction quality among tested architectures (DeepMind paper reports).
Auxiliary loss + extra weights add complexity. Sometimes hard to tune.
JumpReLU SAE: Nearly as good as Gated with simpler architecture. One activation function, no aux loss.
Can be trickier to train: gradient signal to theta is sparse (only when z is near theta).
Most common choice in current SAE research (Anthropic, DeepMind, Neuronpedia default).

'Surprisingly, we find that the D-vs-sparsity graph is STICKY at 1 and 1/2.'
'The 1/2 sticky point corresponds to a precise geometric arrangement where features come in

'Model likes to create SPECIFIC WEIGHT GEOMETRIES and JUMPS between the different configurations.'
ZERO SPARSITY -> feature basis isn't privileged, so the model represents features with
ARBITRARY DIRECTIONS. No reason to distinguish some features from others.
HIGHER SPARSITY -> feature basis becomes privileged. PHASE-TRANSITION to representing some
features in antipodal pairs, and the rest aren't represented.
FURTHER SPARSITY -> transition to different geometries (tetrahedra, pentagons, ...).
'The moral: SUPERPOSITION IS VERY HARD TO PIN DOWN. There are many points between D=0 and D=1.
As an analogy, water has more than 3 phases (many kinds of ice crystals). Neural network features
seem to have many phases within superposition.'

The big ideas that hold across all sections.
Superposition is a bet on sparsity
It's cheap to overload a dimension when features rarely co-occur. Cross-talk between
shared dims rarely hurts. Real LLMs (with sparse features) do dramatic superposition.
ReLU makes neurons privileged (acts elementwise). Linear-only readers make residual
stream NOT privileged. Rows of W_in have identity; rows of resid_stream do not.
n_features > d_hidden -> some dim must carry >1 feature. But polysemanticity does NOT
imply superposition (could just be a bad basis).
Interference between shared features only matters when both fire. Sparser features ->
less co-firing -> more features can safely share a neuron.
W^T W is the story of a bottleneck model
Diagonal = per-feature strength. Off-diagonal = per-pair interference. Pentagon has
+0.31 on 72° pairs. Antipodal has -1. Reading W^T W tells you what the model learned.
Correlated features want ORTHOGONAL (both fire, no interference). Anticorrelated want
||W||_F^2 = sum of squared column norms. Each column norm ~= 1 if represented, 0 if
(tetrahedron). Each sticky point is a regular polytope.
A model with hidden ReLU can bypass ReLU by shifting biases positive. To study
Two features can share ONE neuron with unequal input/output weights, plus a corrective
neuron to fix leakage. Works because terminal ReLU truncates negatives.
Small batch: pack DATAPOINTS. Large batch: pack FEATURES. Test-loss spike between.
SAE = overcomplete + sparse decoding of h
d_sae >> d_hidden. Not compression - SEPARATION. Each active z[i] ideally corresponds
to one feature. Trained on FROZEN toy-model activations.
Shrinkage is a fundamental L1 problem
L1 biases optimal z_i DOWN by lambda/(2*||W_dec_i||^2). Reconstruction systematically
undershoots. Gated + JumpReLU fix by separating gate from magnitude.
Dead latents waste capacity - RESAMPLE them
Reinitialize dead latents to hard examples. Standard practice every 2500 steps early in
training. resample_advanced uses squared loss for weighting.
Gated SAE: two paths + aux loss
f = f_gate * f_mag. L1 on gate only. Aux loss prevents degenerate gate=off. Fixes
z * H(z - theta) with learned theta. Direct L0 penalty. Backprop via rectangle-kernel
STE. Simpler than Gated with comparable performance.
